topic: why metallic paint separates into two cans (leafing behavior)
title: Why Metallic Paint Comes In Two Separate Cans
description: AI-narrated commentary exploring the physics behind why metallic paint is mixed fresh instead of sold pre-combined, and the microscopic trick that gives it its shine.

hook_candidates.text: Why does metallic paint come in two separate cans instead of one?
Metallic paint is only good for a few minutes after it's mixed — then it stops working.
You'd think metallic paint is just glitter in a can. It's actually a physics trick called leafing.

beats.text: Why does metallic paint come in two separate cans instead of one?
Because the shine only shows up for a few minutes after they're combined.
Inside that paint are microscopic aluminum flakes, thinner than tissue paper.
Mix them into varnish, and something strange happens: they don't stay mixed — they float.
The flakes rise and stack flat near the surface, like fish scales lining up in the same direction.
That's called leafing, and it's the only reason the paint looks metallic instead of just gray.
Wait too long after mixing, and the flakes settle to the bottom — the shine is gone for good.
So 'mix before use' isn't a suggestion — it's the whole trick. What else looks ordinary until you know the physics behind it? Tell me your guess.
